articles.title: Will the price caps on cancer drugs help bring down the cost of treatment?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: When Sarojini Nadimpally was diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer in June 2025, the Delhi-based public health researcher was staring at a hidden reality as daunting as the tumour. One dose of the targeted combination drug she had been prescribed would cost around ₹2.7 lakh — and she needed 18 doses.

As someone who works on access to medicines, she closely followed the government’s recent decision to cap trade margins on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs at 30%, extending a 2019 cap that covered 42. The government claims that the cap, which takes effect on November 9, can save patients about ₹2,500 crore a year.
“Any intervention to lower the prices of cancer drugs is a welcome step,” says Ms. Nadimpally. “But it remains to be seen how this cap will actually reduce what patients pay.”

Cancer is said to be India’s leading cause of catastrophic health spending . India’s out-of-pocket share for cancer care — estimated by various studies to be 50%-80% of direct treatment costs — is far higher than in most high-income systems, where insurance or tax-funded care generally absorbs the bulk of these expenses.

Experts say that drugs make up around over half the costs of cancer care. “High costs of treatments such as targeted therapies and immunotherapy can lead many patients to defer treatment, opt for cheaper but less effective alternatives or give up altogether,” says Vedant Kabra, principal director, surgical oncology, Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Gurugram.

When pills threaten to outrun savings , the standard of care is down to a cruel trade-off between effectiveness and affordability. For example, at about ₹1.25 lakh a month, a lifetime course of osimertinib, the drug of choice in fighting EGFR-mutated lung cancer while reducing the risk of brain metastases, is beyond the reach of many. “These patients switch to gefitinib, which costs only about ₹2,500 a month, but return with brain secondaries and disease progression,” says Narayanankutty Warrier, senior consultant oncologist, MVR Cancer Centre and Research Institute, Kozhikode. “About 30% new-generation drugs are really good,” he says. “The rest are mostly claims. But even a slight improvement in survival means they become monopoly drugs.”

With its latest order , the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) is setting a common trade-margin ceiling on a broad range of cancer medicines, including patented, chemotherapy, targeted, immunotherapy, hormonal and blood cancer drugs. Manufacturers are required to report formulation-level information, including brand name, composition, pack size, PTS (price to stockist) and revised MRP.

The order spells out that a drug with a PTS of ₹70 and an MRP of ₹300 can have an MRP of no more than ₹100, excluding GST. Experts argue that the permitted margin — which amounts to 42.8% of the PTS — is a sizeable mark-up, especially for expensive drugs.

In effect, the government is putting a ceiling on the profit, not the underlying price. For example, the actual prices at which hospitals buy drugs, often after steep discounts negotiated for bulk purchases, are hidden from sight. “A cap on trade margins means little to patients if hospitals and dealers do not pass those savings on, and there is no way of knowing whether they do,” says Ms. Nadimpally.

On October 28, the NPPA published a revised price list for the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs based on data submitted by companies. The MRPs of 37 drugs remain unchanged, offering an early indication of what the final list may look like. The list also reveals margins that manufacturers, including some Indian generic makers, have had. For instance, palbociclib’s MRP for one brand is down from about ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 a pack, and thiotepa’s from about ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 a vial — drops of more than 90%.

The latest order also counts the cap from the PTS, not from the ex-factory price or the landed cost (price paid after discounts and freight), leaving out upstream additions. The mark-up for cancer medicines is unjustified, says Malini Aisola, co-convener, All India Drug Action Network. “With few middlemen involved in the distribution of these high-value, low-volume products, a hospital or distributor gets to keep nearly all the margin. That legitimises profiteering.”

When it comes to patented, mostly imported medicines, we are price-takers, insists Ms. Aisola. “The government is averse to using its legal powers under the Indian Patent Act and TRIPS (Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) — such as government use and compulsory licensing — to increase competition.”

articles.title: UNICEF urges media to promote inclusive early childhood development, report responsibly on AI
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The early years of a child’s life are critical for lifelong health, learning, emotional well-being, and social development. Inclusive early childhood development (iECD) seeks to ensure that every child, including those with developmental delays, disabilities, autism and other forms of neurodivergence, has equitable access to healthcare, nutrition, nurturing care, early learning, protection, and early intervention, Deepa Bhaskaran, Director, Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, said.

Speaking at a media workshop on inclusive early childhood development and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for effective storytelling, organised by UNICEF India in association with the Press Information Bureau, Dr. Bhaskaran said early identification and interventions were vital to ensure that children with disabilities and developmental delays were included at home, in learning environments, and in their communities.
“We train and support medical staff and caregivers, improve early identification and intervention, and provide advanced disability inclusive services,” she said.

Amar Fettle, State Nodal Officer for Adolescent Health, speaking at the workshop, added that while medical infrastructure and personnel were geared towards clinical care, research, teaching, and community outreach, it was equally important to shape public understanding of children’s issues and government programmes.

“Families and the public should understand the services available and help reduce the stigma surrounding disability and developmental delays. The idea is to ensure that children are included in society,” Dr. Fettle said.

The workshop aimed to strengthen understanding of inclusive early childhood development, child rights and disability inclusion, promote ethical, child-sensitive and non-stigmatising reporting, and raise awareness of AI-related risks, including misinformation, deepfakes, bias, privacy violations, and fabricated content.

While reporting, subject matter expertise is essential, Muralikrishna Chinnadurai, trainer with the Google News Initiative India Network, said. Relying on a single AI prompt could produce unreliable information, Mr. Chinnadurai said.
“Humans must be in the loop. AI tools should be used ethically and in an environmentally responsible manner,” he said.

articles.title: Small fish: On Operation Trident
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Operation Trident , a multi-agency crackdown on an international syndicate operating across the India-Myanmar-Bangladesh corridor, marks a significant step-up in the government’s campaign against drug trafficking. The Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has set December 31, 2029, as the deadline to eradicate drug networks across the country. The October 23 raids, which led to 18 people being arrested , were based on NCB investigations following the arrest of an alleged Myanmar-based kingpin in Delhi this May. However, the dismantling of the entire network would require identification of all suppliers in Myanmar and their successful prosecution. The government’s strategy, involving States and Union Territories, over 40 Ministries, central agencies and the pharmaceutical sector, is outlined in the Vision Document on Drug Control (2026-2029), launched by Mr. Shah at the Narco-Coordination Centre meeting on June 26, 2026. It envisages dismantling 100 major cartels and improving prosecution outcomes. The broad strategy reflects the complexity of the problem and signals a more focused approach. Data for 2025 also show an increase of over 50% in arrests and a nearly 53% rise in cases registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act compared with 2024.

However, the government’s action-plan will depend on consistent implementation and efficient coordination among agencies, and striking at the real brains behind it all. In several cases, foreign-based key operatives still remain at large and big sharks often do not fall in the net. The 2021 Mundra port case in Gujarat, involving the seizure of about 3,000 kg of heroin, is a case in point wherein the principal Afghanistan-based suppliers have yet to be brought to book. Also, the quantity of drugs seized does not, by itself, indicate whether drug availability or consumption has declined. Punjab remains a prominent example of the continuing public health challenges associated with drug abuse. The alleged drug-related killings of anti-drug activists in Mansa and Gurdaspur, along with the alleged death by suicide of a father in Sangrur who had raised concerns about the easy availability of synthetic drugs in his locality, underscore the human cost of the problem. These incidents also raise questions about the protection of those who speak out against drug trafficking and networks. These concerns lend urgency to the objective of dismantling entire networks and apprehending the “big sharks”, rather than concentrating disproportionately on individual carriers. The key is to identify the ultimate beneficiaries by meticulously following the money trail and ensuring their conviction.

articles.title: Fouled waters: On Rajasthan’s river pollution
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Supreme Court has pulled up, once again, the Rajasthan government over industrial effluents flowing into the Jojari river and the deadly risk it poses for the people depending on it. The problem is decades old — public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court alerted State machinery to the problem in 2011 — indicating an oversight by the State bordering on the systematic. The Jojari, the Luni, and the Bandi are seasonal rivers in the State’s arid western region, flowing through Jodhpur, Balotra, and Pali districts. This region has also evolved as a textile-dyeing and steelworking hub, and untreated or insufficiently treated effluents from these factories have run directly into the rivers and soil, endangering the health of around 20 lakh local residents. The region also suffers rampant illegal sand mining in riverbeds. The sewage treatment plants have been able to accommodate only around half of the sewage generated in the three urban centres, according to the State’s submissions to the Court in 2025, even as the Court recorded substantial underutilisation at common effluent treatment plants. The combination is suggestive of industrial sources bypassing treatment facilities, poor connections between the sources and the facilities, and/or insufficient capacity at particular sites or in specific periods.

The Court initiated a suo motu writ petition in 2025 and constituted a High-level Ecosystem Oversight Committee chaired by Justice Sangeet Lodha to audit the plants and draft a plan to restore the rivers. Based on the committee’s scathing status reports, Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta banned construction within 100 metres of the rivers’ edges and hazardous industries within 500 m of the present path, or of the flood lines where available. The Court has also upbraided local authorities for failing to enforce pollution norms by citing the Court’s own stay of a 2022 National Green Tribunal order imposing a compensation on the Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation and the local administration in Jodhpur and Barmer. The State regulatory apparatus has been dysfunctional: officials were aware of illegal mining operations in some areas, yet they regularised leases in those areas. Given the dereliction in play, the Court is correct to treat the possibility of collusion between State officials and industrial mafias seriously. Justice Mehta’s observation that the State could be held liable under the ‘polluter pays’ principle is also a significant indictment of state failure, through negligence. Now, importantly, the State still has to restore the Jojari and attend to its wellbeing, which is relevant to a recent tendency by the Court to substitute itself for regulators rather than disciplining them into discharging their functions. This needs to change.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: On the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: A final surge: On Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

• Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

articles.title: Wicked surprise: On the northeast monsoon
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: As India recovers from a monsoon-deficit year , there is both hope and trepidation regarding the prospects for that ‘other monsoon’, or the ‘northeast monsoon’ . While contributing only around a quarter of India’s annual rainfall, it is largely focused on the south-east peninsula regions of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Keralam. The southwest monsoon, influenced by a strengthening El Niño , has already left its desiccating mark. Rainfall from June-September was 759.4 mm against 868.6 mm, a 12.6% deficit, the driest in 11 years. This has impacted kharif sowing and is reflected in food inflation.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said that this year, the northeast monsoon rainfall, spanning October to December, would likely be ‘normal’ , meaning in line with a 50-year average and within a 12% error window. Most parts of the country, it said, are expected to receive below-normal rainfall, except some areas of northwest India and southern parts of peninsular India, where rainfall is likely to be normal to above-normal. The wide error window, however, is far less precise than its forecasts for the southwest monsoon with its margin of 5%, and can sometimes make the northeast monsoon the bearer of nasty surprises. For instance, December 1, 2015, saw the city of Chennai deluged by its heaviest rainfall in 24-hours in over a century ; at least 500 lives were lost and 18 lakh people displaced in the State. That year and the present are linked by a common thread: a powerful El Niño. Associated with the heating up of the Central Pacific, the El Niño is linked to the drying up of the southwest monsoon rains but also yoked — not always — with a vigorous northeast monsoon. Other than in 2015, several El Niño years, such as 1997 and 2009, have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu though El Niño years, such as 2002 and 1982, saw a poor northeast monsoon (and a predictably bad southwest monsoon). While the climate mechanisms linking a vigorous northeast monsoon and El Niño are still to be fully understood, it appears the warming patterns of the El Niño tend to deflect rain-bearing cyclonic circulations in unpredictable ways. Therefore, the Centre and the southern States ought to take enough precautions: from clearing up stormwater drains, fortifying shelters, making provisions for infrastructure damage and tightening weather warning forecasts to prepare for torrents.

articles.title: Old values, new avenues: On India-Poland ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Sixteen years after his visit as Poland’s Prime Minister, Donald Tusk’s travel to Delhi and Bengaluru last week was to signal a renewed desire to work closely with India. Mr. Tusk’s visit, two months ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s trip to Brussels to sign the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement , indicated one part of his agenda. Both sides agreed that it was time to develop trade, currently worth just $6 billion, to double its size by 2030. Mr. Tusk’s last visit to India was in 2017, as President of the European Council for the EU-India summit, and it is fitting that his trip was just as the FTA is finalised and ratified after years of delays. Another area of increased India-Poland collaboration is in technology, AI and defence hardware, critical minerals, renewable and nuclear energy given Poland’s expertise in the last few decades and India’s capacity for scale. As the EU’s sixth largest economy, Poland has officially crossed the $1 trillion GDP (nominal terms) milestone. Its $120-billion-dollar tech economy is also gaining global interest. A large part of Polish machinery and parts is exported to Germany, which in turn has a growing share of Indian imports, and India could consider more trilateral collaborations for manufacturing and mining technology. The two sides agreed to establish a “Defence Industry Dialogue” and explore a dialogue on counter-terrorism cooperation. Finally, the Modi-Tusk talks focused on geopolitics, particularly the ongoing war in Ukraine. The war’s impact, especially on the Global South, has been a concern for India, and the Modi government’s initiative to work on an agreement acceptable to Kyiv and Moscow on grain exports and seafarers’ safety was discussed. The four-pronged plan, announced by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during his September visit to Warsaw, won Mr. Tusk’s support.

At the India-Poland Business Forum in Bengaluru, Mr. Tusk, who was accompanied by a Polish business delegation, said the challenge now was in “translating” the talks and MoUs signed into actual joint ventures between businesses. Apart from the distance and geographies, there is the matter of trust, given India’s defence engagement with Russia and Poland’s defence ties with Pakistan. Poland is credited with training Pakistan’s Air Force in its early years; a mutual defence cooperation agreement was signed in 2018. India has a unique and enduring partnership with Russia, and New Delhi is unlikely to accept Warsaw’s strictures over its military engagement and exercises with Russia that caused a controversy earlier this year during the Polish Foreign Minister’s visit. It is essential for Delhi and Warsaw to complete the confidentiality of classified information that is still being negotiated and draw up the parameters of future cooperation based on realities. Mr. Tusk’s statement that India and Poland today have no “conflicts of interest” is a significant aspiration, for two countries that share old values, and new avenues of partnership.

articles.title: Cyclone ‘Arnab’: Flights, trains cancelled as rain batters A.P.; 30,000 boats brought ashore; southern Odisha on edge
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Heavy rain pounded the northern districts of Andhra Pradesh on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), leaving one dead and a trail of destruction, while southern Odisha remained on edge as the ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ Arnab moved closer to the coast.

According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the storm is likely to make landfall early — around 2 a.m. to 4 a.m. on Wednesday (October 28) – near the Yanam-Kakinada region in Andhra Pradesh. Initially, the IMD had said that the landfall would take place around forenoon on Wednesday.
Keep track | Cyclone ‘Arnab’ LIVE updates | Storm 140 km from Kakinada; highest danger signal hoisted at Kakinada port

According to real-time information from the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES), Jathara premises in Visakhapatnam rural mandal recorded Tuesday’s (October 27) highest rainfall of 141.75 mm between 8.30 a.m. and 7 p.m. Visakhapatnam district, where many places experienced rainfall above 100 mm and strong winds, bore the brunt of the cyclone. At least 200 trees were uprooted within the city limits.

A 65-year-old man died at Mangalapalem after he came into contact with live electrical wires that had snapped and fallen into water. The districts of Vizianagaram, Anakapalli, and Srikakulam also recorded widespread rainfall of above 80 mm until 7 p.m. on Tuesday.

As per the latest information from the IMD, the storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal is moving at a speed higher than expected. As of 5.30 p.m., it was located around 90 km southeast of Kakinada, 170 km south of Visakhapatnam, 170 km east of Machilipatnam, 240 km east-northeast of Bapatla, and 380 km south-southwest of Gopalpur in Odisha.

IMD, Amaravati, Director K. Nagaratnam, who is monitoring the cyclone situation along with her team from Vijayawada, said the rainfall activity, which is centred around northern districts in the morning, would shift to the districts of Kakinada, West and East Godavari, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema by Tuesday night, when the system moves northwestwards towards Yanam.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Cyclone Arnab: What Andhra Pradesh needs to know

Due to the increasing severity of the storm on Tuesday (October 27), airlines cancelled at least 21 flights in Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam. At the Vijayawada airport, five flights bound for Hyderabad, Chennai, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam, and Kadapa were cancelled on Tuesday (October 27). The authorities have cancelled all flights on Wednesday as well.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu said 290 cyclone shelters had been set up and 84,396 people evacuated to safer locations. More than 30,000 fishing boats had been brought back from the sea, while 93 Andhra Pradesh boats and their crew were reported safe at Gopalpur in Odisha.

The State has mobilised 8,400 personnel to respond to electricity disruptions and is prepared for the possible collapse of up to 15,000 power poles. Teams from the National and State Disaster Response Force, the Navy and the Coast Guard had also been alerted.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) Managing Director Prakhar Jain have advised the public to be alert, as extremely heavy rain is expected on Tuesday night in the districts of Kakinada, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, and Anakapalli. In cases of emergency, one can dial toll-free helplines 1070, 112, or 18004250101.

fullParagraphs: Traffic on Ennore Expressway and other coastal roads in north Chennai and Tiruvallur district witnessed high waves lashing onto the land as a result of cyclone Arnab on Tuesday evening (October 27, 2026). Residents of Kasikoilkuppam, Ennore, Tiruvottiyur, Bharathi Nagar and Ramakrishna Nagar came out of their homes in panic, seeing the storm surge. Tiruvottiyur MLA N. Senthil Kumar, who visited the spot, said that there was no need for the public to panic. Andhra Pradesh prepares for Cyclone Arnab: evacuations, travel cancellations, shelters activated, with expert insight on landfall and severest impacts.

Cyclone Arnab has uprooted 206 trees across Visakhapatnam, and the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) had cleared 55 of them by 6 p.m. on Tuesday. Thirty tree-clearing teams are working to reopen blocked roads.

GVMC Commissioner Ketan Garg inspected parts of the East and South zones on his way to Gajuwaka and asked officials to stay in the field and clear fallen trees and debris at once. Sanitation workers have been asked to work through the night.

Only about 2,000 people in Yanam have moved to relief camps so far, with most residents unwilling to leave their homes despite repeated warnings, officials said on Tuesday. The Puducherry enclave, close to where the cyclone is expected to cross the coast, has set up 20 relief camps for nearly 5,000 people.

“Most of them are not willing to move to the relief camps, forcing us to deploy NDRF personnel and local police to persuade them,” Yanam Regional Administrator Shivraj Meena told The Hindu . About 100 NDRF personnel are stationed in Yanam, home to more than 55,600 people, and trees along roads have been trimmed to limit damage.

A 65-year-old man died at Mangalapalem in Visakhapatnam on Tuesday after he allegedly came into contact with live electrical wires that had snapped and fallen into water. A. Pinni Devudu was walking through the water and was apparently unaware of the fallen lines, sources said. The Duvvada police have shifted the body to King George Hospital.

Sixteen flights were cancelled at the Visakhapatnam airport and five at the Vijayawada airport on Tuesday, officials said. The Vijayawada cancellations, four by IndiGo and one by Air India Express, hit services to Chennai, Bengaluru, Visakhapatnam and Kadapa.
Fifteen flights have already been cancelled at Vijayawada for Wednesday, including all 12 IndiGo services, Fly91’s flights and Air India’s morning flight to Delhi, an airport official said.

The Ranchi district administration in Jharkhand has closed schools on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) and Thursday after a rain alert. Eight to nine districts of the State are likely to be affected by the cyclone, Ranchi Meteorological Centre Deputy Director Abhishek Anand said.

The Andaman and Nicobar administration has told fishermen not to venture into the sea till Wednesday (October 28, 2026) and asked operators of tourism and recreational activities on land and at sea to be careful. Rain is expected in all three districts of the islands till October 29, and people in low-lying areas have been asked to stay alert.

Mahalingam of Kasikoilkuppam said that water had entered their village. It is a scary situation, he added. The National Highways Authority of India closed the expressway to traffic after vehicles were drenched in the waves. Smaller vehicles were pushed due to the force of the waves. Some fishermen thought the waves could be a due to a tsunami and wanted to find if there was any earthquake.

Ennore traffic police have diverted vehicles along two routes. Vehicles from Ramakrishna Nagar to Annai Sivagami Nagar are being diverted via Ernavur Bridge, Murugar Kovil Road and Kathivakkam Beach. Vehicles from Thazhakuppam and Ennore are being diverted via Kathivakkam Bridge and Murugar Kovil road, police said.

In Tiruvallur district, the Collector S. Kavitha has pressed the police, fire services and the revenue department to ensure the safety of the public living along the coast. The Regional Meteorological Centre here had warned of rough seas due to the cyclone. The sea is expected to calm down by noon on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).

articles.title: SSB chief to take additional charge of ITBP as D-G retires

fullParagraphs: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has assigned the additional charge of Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) to Sanjay Singhal, who heads the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), with effect from October 31, when incumbent Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor retires. The ITBP guards India’s 3,488-km border with China.

On October 22, Mr. Kapoor said at an ITBP event in Rajasthan’s Alwar that “face-offs with Chinese troops continue at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh,” leading to a political uproar and demands by the Opposition parties for clarity on the extent of Chinese incursion in the eastern sector.

Mr. Kapoor said, “In the past few days, a situation arose where face-offs happened at several locations in Arunachal, and it still continues. Our Shaurya commandos played an exemplary role in this. ITBP was raised as a mountain guerrilla force, and we were given border guarding duty along China in 2004. We need not leave our original function, and a specialised high-altitude mountain fighting force is being set up, distinct from the Army. We will soon have one full battalion of Shaurya commandos. High-altitude (deployment) is our strength,” Mr. Kapur said.
This was the first official confirmation of the scale of tensions along the northeastern border since July.

On Tuesday (October 27), an MHA order said, “The undersigned is directed to refer to the subject mentioned above and to convey the approval of competent authority for assignment of additional charge of the post of D-G, ITBP to Sanjay Singhal, IPS (UP:1993), D-G, SSB upon superannuation of Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, IPS (HY:1990) on 31.10.2026 and till the appointment of a regular incumbent or until further orders, whichever is earlier.”

articles.title: U.P. Chief Electoral Officer apologises for ‘tone, language and sharpness’ of social media posts
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The office of the Chief Electoral Officer of Uttar Pradesh on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) apologised over the “tone” and tenor of social media posts made by the poll body, following a row over the acerbic nature of the remarks, which pertained to erroneous voter slip entries.

The controversy began when Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) MP Sanjay Singh questioned Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over an erroneous entry, where ‘Ramhit Yadav’ became ‘Ram ne Yadav ko Maara’ (Ram hit Yadav) in the voter list of the recent Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council election.

U.P. Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa’s office attributed the error to a translation software glitch. The software used to prepare voter lists was designed to transliterate names entered in English into Hindi, which led to ‘Ramhit Yadav’ being incorrectly entered as ‘Ram Hit Yadav’. The software interpreted the words as a sentence and translated it to “Ram ne Yadav ko Maara” in Hindi.

Mr. Singh had questioned the CEC on whether the latter was running the agenda for a particular political party. “Gyanesh Kumar, why did Ram hit only a Yadav? Why did Ram not hit any Singh, Pathak, Asthana, Sharma, Rai or Bisht? Is your computer casteist? Are you running the agenda of any political party?” the AAP leader said in a post on social media platform X.
In an acerbic response, Mr. Rinwa’s office cited another instance of a similar error, where the name of the father of a voter, Ravi Sharma, was incorrectly recorded as “Ram ne Sharma ko Maara”.

“A bizarre name, ‘Ram ne Sharma ko maara’, has appeared in the voter list for the recent Legislative Council elections. Computers/software are not casteist. We admit that a mistake was made, but fortunately for us, even when the mistake occurred, caste discrimination was not involved,” Mr. Rinwa’s office said.

This was followed by another mocking remark by Mr. Rinwa’s office, which said that had the entry read “Ram hit a minority”, the authorities would have been accused of communalism too. “Thank God, Ram did not kill a member of a minority community. Otherwise, we would have been accused of being communal as well as casteist,” the remark read.

The AAP MP was quick to hit back. On Monday (October 26, 2026), he held a press conference in Lucknow, alleging that the U.P. Chief Electoral Officer was responding like an “agent of the BJP”. He also flagged other absurd entries in the electoral rolls, and sought strict action against Mr. Rinwa for the objectionable remarks.

On Tuesday (October 27, 2026), however, Mr. Rinwa’s office issued an apology. “The tone, language and sharpness of the comments in the quoted post from this handle are not in keeping with the kind of communication expected from an official handle,” the apology posted to X said.

“The genuine outrage sparked by the comments in the post has been duly noted. We sincerely apologise to those who have been shocked and angered by them. From now on, our communication will be civil and formal,” Mr. Rinwa’s office said.

articles.title: Focus on early intervention at UNICEF workshop on inclusive child development
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Inclusive early childhood development comprises systems that should reach every child, including those with special needs for whom early interventions can make a significant difference, Vivek Virendra Singh, Lead – Health, Communication Specialist, UNICEF India, has said. He was speaking at a media workshop on ‘Inclusive early childhood development’ organised by UNICEF in association with Press Information Bureau here on Tuesday.

Dr. Singh pointed out that 3% to 10% of the nearly 4 lakh children born in the State could have special needs. He also spoke about district early intervention centres for multi-sectoral interventions for children with special needs.

Deepa Bhaskaran, director, Child Development Centre, Thiruvananthapuram, in a session on ‘Parenting children with spectrum disabilities’ spoke about intervening when the first signs of autism are identified rather than wait for more to appear. Avoiding eye gaze, not responding to being called by name by six to nine months, or not babbling by 12 months were all things that mothers should look out for, she said. She spoke about how to parent children on the spectrum, teaching them emotions, regulating emotions not only of the children but also of parents, coping toolkit, and everyday strategies.

Amar Fettle, State Nodal Officer for Adolescent Health, National Health Mission, spoke on building an inclusive health system, from the primary and family health centre upwards to the CDC, and how these along with systems such as Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) helped in assessment of children and providing appropriate interventions.

Muralikrishna Chinnadurai, trainer, Google News Initiative India Network and AI expert, conducted a session on ‘Using AI for effective storytelling.’ Syam Sudheer Pandi, communications specialist, UNICEF also spoke.

articles.title: Coal India H1 capital expenditure surges 27% to ₹7,966-cr, exceeds target
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: State-owned Coal India Ltd (CIL) increased its capital expenditure by 27% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹7,966 crore in the first half of the current financial year, exceeding its stipulated target of ₹7,286 crore for the period.

The miner has utilised more than 48% of its annual capital expenditure outlay of ₹16,500 crore, reflecting a strong investment push towards strengthening mining infrastructure, expanding operational capacity and improving coal evacuation.
Mine infrastructure development, land acquisition, plant and machinery, and diversification together accounted for 79% of the expenditure during the April-September period.

“These strategic investments are expected to strengthen the company’s operational capabilities and support the achievement of its production and supply targets for the ongoing financial year,” Coal India said.

Mine infrastructure development accounted for the largest share of capital expenditure at ₹2,152 crore. The investments were directed primarily towards strengthening coal evacuation and handling infrastructure, including railway sidings and corridors, coal handling plants (CHPs), silos and weighbridges.

Land acquisition was the second-largest expenditure head, accounting for ₹2,033 crore during the first half. The company also spent more than ₹1,000 crore on mine development to facilitate the expansion and operational readiness of mining projects.

The Kolkata-headquartered miner invested ₹1,394 crore in plant and machinery (P&M), including ₹452 crore towards the purchase of heavy earth-moving machinery (HEMM). The remaining expenditure was incurred on washeries and other plant and machinery.

With nearly half of its annual capital expenditure already deployed, Coal India’s investment programme is focused on augmenting mining capacity and addressing potential infrastructure bottlenecks that can constrain production and coal movement. The emphasis on evacuation infrastructure is particularly significant as the company seeks to align its production and supply targets with the capacity to transport coal efficiently.

articles.title: Nayara Energy hikes petrol by ₹5, diesel by ₹3
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Nayara Energy, India's largest private fuel retailer, has raised petrol prices by ₹5 per litre and diesel by ₹3 with immediate effect, seeking to narrow the gap between retail prices and rising international oil and refined-product costs, people familiar with the matter said.

The latest increase comes amid renewed pressure on fuel retailers from higher global energy prices and follows a series of price adjustments by Nayara this year as refiners grapple with the impact of geopolitical disruptions on crude and product markets.
Nayara, which operates 7,108 petrol pumps across the country, raised petrol and diesel prices with effect from early hours of Saturday (October 3, 2026), sources said.
An email sent to Nayara spokesperson for comments remained unanswered.

Nayara was the first fuel retailer to pass on the surge in international oil prices to consumers when the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies earlier this year. On March 26, it raised petrol prices by ₹5 a litre and diesel by ₹3, taking the rates at its outlets to ₹100.71 and ₹91.31 a litre, respectively, at the time.
State-owned fuel retailers subsequently began raising pump prices in May.

They increased petrol and diesel prices in a series of staggered moves, with the cumulative increase reaching about ₹7.50 a litre each by late May. The fourth increase on May 25 was ₹2.61 a litre for petrol and ₹2.71 for diesel.

Nayara later reversed its March increase. On July 1, the company cut petrol prices by ₹5 a litre and diesel by ₹3, after international crude prices eased as tensions in West Asia subsided. The reduction was the first by a fuel retailer in more than two years and brought Nayara's pricing broadly back in line with state-owned retailers.
The latest hike, therefore, marks a renewed attempt by the private retailer to pass through higher costs after a period of relatively subdued retail prices.

State-owned oil marketing companies - Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation - control more than 90% of the country's 1,04,137 fuel petrol pumps and have historically kept pump prices relatively stable even when international crude prices fluctuate.
The pricing gap has become increasingly consequential for fuel retailers.
On October 1, the government said private retailers should not cap petrol and diesel sales at their outlets, after Nayara and Jio-bp restricted volumes at some pumps amid losses on retail sales.

articles.title: What the new E100 vehicle rules mean | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The story so far: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 , to permit the use of ethanol-based fuels containing up to 100% ethanol (E100) in vehicles. The move paves the way for flex-fuel vehicles, which can run on petrol, ethanol blends of varying proportions, or pure ethanol.
The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing.

One of the key changes is the inclusion of E100, or fuel comprising 100% ethanol, alongside E85 in several tables under Rule 115. E85 is a fuel containing up to 85% ethanol, while E100 consists entirely of ethanol, subject to applicable fuel specifications.
The amendments include an explanatory note stating that E85 or E100 may be used only in flex-fuel vehicles designed by original equipment manufacturers.

No. In a press statement, the Ministry sought to allay concerns among motorists, clarifying that a vehicle’s compatibility with E10 or E20 does not establish its suitability for E85. The notification does not require owners of existing vehicles to switch to E85 or modify their vehicles, either now or in the future.

Motorists should check the fuel-compatibility sticker on their vehicle and follow the manufacturer’s guidance in the owner’s manual when choosing fuel at a filling station, the Ministry statement added.

The amendments are expected to facilitate homologation, the official certification process through which authorised agencies, such as the Automotive Research Association of India, verify that vehicles and components comply with technical, safety and environmental standards before they can be approved for sale or use on public roads.
This will help secure type approvals for E100-powered vehicles, supporting their rollout and wider consumer adoption.
Corrections have also been incorporated into fuel classifications, including a reference to gasoline blended with 20% ethanol, or E20, in place of an earlier notation referring to E10.

India achieved its 20% ethanol-blending (E20) target in 2025 , five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. From April 2026, all Bharat Stage-VI (BS-VI) vehicles are required to fully meet E20 emission standards, and all petrol sold across India is mandated to contain 20% ethanol (E20). The policy focus is now widening beyond E20: the government has enabled the regulatory pathway for E85 and E100 vehicles, though these fuels will require compatible flex-fuel vehicles and dedicated dispensing infrastructure.

The main concern is vehicle compatibility. Owners of older or non-E20-compliant vehicles question whether E20 could damage components, raise maintenance costs, or leave them without access to lower-ethanol petrol.

Consumers also question E20’s effect on fuel economy. Ethanol has a lower energy density than petrol; while the government estimates a 5% decline in mileage, some consumers say the loss is greater. Dealers, meanwhile, warn that ethanol’s affinity for water could raise contamination risks during the monsoon, strengthening the case for separate storage and dispensing systems for higher blends. These concerns have prompted calls for a transparent assessment.

articles.title: India poised to refine for world as global capacity declines: Union Minister Hardeep Puri
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: India is poised to strengthen its position as a global refining hub, with its oil processing capacity set to rise to 300 million tonnes annually by 2030 even as Europe and other parts of the Western world see refinery capacity decline, Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

India's refining capacity is currently around 290 million tonnes per annum and is expected to expand further by scaling up existing facilities and adding new projects, the Union Petroleum Minister said at a news conference on the sidelines of the 29th Energy Technology and Innovation Meet in south Goa.

He said the expansion will allow India not only to meet its domestic energy requirements but also to supply more petroleum products to international markets. "With refining capacity increasing in a big way, we will be in the happy situation of not only refining for ourselves, but for the world," Mr. Puri added.

He contrasted India's expanding refining infrastructure with the decline in global capacity, particularly in Europe, where he estimated that at least 2,50,000 barrels per day of refining capacity was being lost annually.

"Others are going down. Ours is going up," the minister said, pointing to the expansion of Indian refineries at a time when smaller and less efficient facilities in other markets are struggling with logistical costs and operational inefficiencies.
Mr. Puri said India's refining capacity would reach 300 million tonnes per annum by 2030, though the projection may not include all new greenfield refineries in the pipeline.

He said several existing refineries are expanding capacity, with facilities of three million tonnes per annum scaling up to six million tonnes and those with six million tonnes expanding to nine million tonnes.
The Minister also cited the expansion plans of individual refiners to underline India's ability to increase supplies of petroleum products, including diesel, to both domestic and overseas markets.

Responding to questions on whether India would need to restrict exports to ensure domestic availability, Mr. Puri said the country's expanding production capacity would enable it to cater to both markets. "We are in a position to supply more to domestic and more to outside," he said.

Mr. Puri said Indian refiners had been planning capacity and production increases even when domestic diesel consumption growth was subdued, allowing the industry to prepare for higher output as demand patterns evolve.
He also pointed to the absence of new greenfield refineries in the Western world in recent decades, contrasting it with India's continued investments in refining infrastructure.

The Minister said the government's policy direction and the expansion of India's energy sector would further strengthen the country's position in global markets. "Beyond conventional petroleum products, initiatives such as Samudra Manthan and GOBARdhan (Galvanising Organic Bio-Agro Resources Dhan) are also expected to gain momentum, he said, adding that these developments would complement the country's expanding energy infrastructure.

articles.title: IndusInd Bank posts profit of ₹1,242 crores in Q2; asset quality improvement and interest income drives growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: IndusInd Bank Limited posted a net profit of ₹1,242 crore for the quarter ended September, up 20% sequentially and trimming net loss of ₹437 for the same quarter in the preceding year. The bank had incurred net loss for the same period in previous year due to an increase in microfinance provisioning and write-offs.

The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago. Sequentially, interest income declined by 2%. NII for half year (H1FY27) rose to ₹9,254, up 2.3% on year.

Asset quality of the bank improved substantially, with gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio at 2.73% compared to 3.60% on year and net NPA declining to 0.83% from 1.04% in Q2FY26. However, the net interest margin of the bank slipped to 3.23% from 3.32% a year ago.

Net revenue of the bank for the period rose to ₹6,817 crores compared to ₹6,00 crores a year. A decline in operating expenses also helped push the bottom-line numbers, with expenses slipping to ₹3,943 crores in July-Septemeber from ₹4,013 crore for the same period last year.
Deposits of the bank rose 10% year-on-year to ₹4.28 crores. Advances of the bank for the period stood at 3.63 crores.
IndusInd held provisions of $9,012 crore as of September 30, with the provision coverage ratio at 70%.

IndusInd Bank raised nearly $3.5 billion via the Reserve Bank of India’s special window for foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) account, which was impacted the contraction in NIM. The bank said recovery in margin related to FCNR-B is expected over the next two quarters.

“Q2 reflects the growing strength of the IndusInd Bank franchise and the progress we have made in rebuilding momentum across the business. Our Q2 results demonstrate that the growth has strengthened, profitability has improved, asset quality trends remain encouraging, and our funding profile is becoming more granular and resilient,” Rajiv Anand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of IndusInd Bank said.

The bank also informed the exchanges on Friday (October 23, 2026) that the Board of Directors of the lender has appointed Priyanka Sinha as an Additional Director in the category of Non-Executive Independent Director for a period of four consecutive years, till October 22, 2030.

Speaking to the media at post-earnings conference call, the bank said it remains confident of reaching a 1% exit return on assets for FY27. Bank also expects loans growth momentum to continue driven by retail and wholesale lending. Shares of IndusInd Bank Ltd closed at ₹835.00 on Friday, down 1.76%, on the BSE.

articles.title: BPCL shifts crude sourcing towards Middle East as Russian oil loses price edge
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) tapped more into Middle Eastern crude as Russian oil lost its price advantage and also due to rising freight costs, with the shift becoming more pronounced in November, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, Director (Finance), told analysts during a post-results call on Monday.

“Our spot crude share remained at around 67% in the second quarter, while Russian grade accounted for approximately 37% of our total crude procurement, both broadly in line with the previous quarter,” Mr. Gupta said, adding that the company increased purchases from the Middle East as supplies from the region improved.

Russia accounted for 37% of BPCL’s crude basket in the September quarter, followed by Saudi Arabia at 19%, Abu Dhabi at 17%, the U.S. at 9% and Oman at 6%. The remaining supplies came from countries contributing 1-4% each.
As of September-end, BPCL held about 22 days of crude inventory, with sourcing requirements tied up through December.
Mr. Gupta said the share of Russian crude in October was expected to remain “more or less the same”, although procurement volumes would be lower for November.

“October, our requirement from Russia slightly came down but in the month of November, the cargoes from Russia significantly reduced due to [reduced] commercial viability [compared to that from Middle East], mainly the increase in the freight,” he said, adding that the company did not receive attractive offers for Russian crude in November.

Russian crude was available at a premium of $12-$13 per barrel over benchmark prices in October. The premium has narrowed to $1-$2 per barrel for December cargoes, Mr. Gupta said, although freight costs remain high.
“Maybe today, Russian cargo is preferable than a Middle Eastern cargo for December month because November [procurement] we have already concluded,” he said.

BPCL also diversified its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sourcing during the quarter. Supplies from the Arab Gulf improved, while the US accounted for about 48% of LPG imports in the September quarter.
Softening Saudi Contract Prices (Saudi CP), the benchmark for LPG pricing, helped reduce under-recoveries to an average ₹290 per cylinder in the September quarter from ₹507 in the June quarter.

Under-recoveries are expected to be ₹245 per cylinder in October and are expected to rise to ₹328 in November, Mr. Gupta said. BPCL currently holds 32 days of LPG inventory, including supplies in transit.
The company has also diversified liquefied natural gas (LNG) procurement by increasing spot purchases from the US, Oman and West Africa.

articles.title: Explosions heard over Riyadh as Saudi authorities say Houthi missiles downed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Saudi authorities said they destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen after explosions were heard over the Saudi capital Riyadh on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).
They said air defences destroyed another three Houthi ballistic missiles fired toward the country's eastern region.
Meanwhile, the Houthis accused government forces of killing two people in a strike at a gas station near the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz, where fighting has been intensifying between the two sides.

For weeks, the Houthis have largely encircled Taiz — the capital of Taiz province and Yemen's third-largest city — and cut off most supply routes from government-held areas, but government forces have fought back.

articles.title: Attacks kill at least 60 Orthodox Christians in Ethiopia, church says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Two attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia region killed at least 60 Orthodox Christians, the country's Orthodox Church said, urging authorities to protect civilians and bring those responsible to justice.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod said Monday (October 26, 2026) that 14 people were killed in Merti district on Oct. 20 and a further 46 in Shirka district on Oct. 24. Both districts are in Oromia's Arsi Zone.
More than 20 people were seriously wounded, and 20 homes were burned down, the church said, describing the killings as “brutal and merciless massacres.”

Oromia regional government spokesperson Hailu Adugna blamed the Oromo Liberation Army for the attacks. He accused the rebels and their allies of trying to provoke ethnic and religious conflict to divert attention from military losses in northern Ethiopia. He presented no evidence supporting the accusations in the statement.
Adugna expressed sorrow over the deaths and destruction and said regional authorities had begun taking action against those responsible. He pledged assistance to people wounded or displaced.
The OLA could not be reached for comment. Its leader, Jaal Marroo, denied that his fighters target civilians in an interview with The Associated Press published in February.
“Our war is not against the people,” he said at the time.

The OLA is one of seven groups in the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, formed in September with the aim of removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Other members include the Tigray People's Liberation Front and the Amhara Fano National Movement.
The church said the attacks violated constitutional protections for religious freedom and the right to life. It called on authorities to publicly condemn the killings and prevent further violence.

Oromia, Ethiopia's largest region and home to roughly 40 million people, has endured a conflict between government forces and the OLA since 2018. Other armed groups and criminal gangs also operate there, with civilians facing killings, extortion and kidnapping.

United Nations investigators have accused the OLA of killings, rapes and kidnappings. Human rights monitors have also documented abuses by government forces, including indiscriminate drone strikes, extrajudicial killings and disappearances.

Sarah Kimani, Amnesty International's media manager, told the AP in a January interview that the organisation's research documents summary executions, torture, abductions and rape by both government forces and the OLA.

articles.title: Norway, Finland leaders hold 'frank and substantive' talk with Putin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Finland's President and Norway's Prime Minister held a "frank and substantive" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) about efforts to end the war in Ukraine, the Nordic leaders said.
It was the latest effort by Kyiv's allies to de-escalate the most deadly conflict in Europe since World War II, which erupted when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our security and broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," President Alexander Stubb said in a joint statement with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.

Speaking to reporters in Helsinki, Mr. Stubb said the idea for the call had originated during a meeting in Oslo on October 20 between Store, Mr. Stubb and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also took part in the meeting remotely. After the Oslo talks, Witkoff travelled to Saint Petersburg to meet Mr. Putin.

Mr. Stubb said, "Both the Americans and the Ukrainians thought it would be a good idea to reach out," and that Ukraine had wished for the Nordic countries to help it "open a channel of communication".
Store, who was also in Helsinki for a meeting of Nordic leaders, told reporters that the 90-minute call had highlighted "big differences in views" on Ukraine.
According to a statement from the Kremlin, Mr. Putin had during the call stressed that it was the EU's and NATO's "confrontational policy" that was "leading to a protraction of hostilities".
The Kremlin said the three leaders had "agreed to continue maintaining direct contact by telephone".
Mr. Stubb described the discussion between the three as "frank and substantive".
Shortly after the announcement of the call, Kyiv said Mr. Zelensky had spoken to the Nordic leaders about the conversation with Mr. Putin.
The Nordic leaders stressed they were only representing their own countries and had not spoken on behalf of Europe, but Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen bemoaned that they had gone "solo".

articles.title: Record turnout as Israeli voters deliver verdict on Netanyahu
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Israelis flocked to the polls Tuesday (October 27, 2026) in record numbers as a deeply divided electorate delivered a verdict on veteran right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the first election since the October 7, 2023 attack.

After casting his vote in Jerusalem, Mr. Netanyahu expressed worry over high voting among Israel's Arab minority and warned of attempts to "steal the election", a signal of a potential long fight ahead as he echoed his ally U.S. President Donald Trump.

Nationwide turnout as of 2:00 p.m. (1200 GMT) was the highest at that point in the day since such statistics were first recorded in 1973, with the Central Elections Committee giving a figure of 44.9%.

Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of October 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.

The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.

The last opinion polls to be published showed Mr. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, running neck and neck with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.
Mr. Eisenkot's Yashar party on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) warned that Mr. Netanyahu was "laying the groundwork to challenge the results" of the election.
Before voting, the 66-year-old military man paid his respects privately at the grave of his son Gal, whose death fighting in Gaza has drawn empathy from many Israelis.
Speaking afterwards at a polling station, Mr. Eisenkot called on Israelis to ignore distractions and vote to replace "the worst government since the state was established".

Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she had lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a centre-right party in Mr. Eisenkot's bloc.
"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.

articles.title: Jaishankar to travel to U.S. for G20 Foreign Ministers’ meet, Quad this week
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A week after United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India , External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar will travel to the U.S. city of Atlanta to attend the meeting of G20 Foreign Ministers hosted by Mr. Rubio. The three-day visit from October 29 to 31, which is Mr. Jaishankar’s fourth trip to the U.S. this year, will include meetings with his counterparts from other G20 countries amidst a series of global developments and the ongoing conflict in West Asia.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has not announced the visit thus far, but diplomatic sources confirmed that his engagements will include the Quad Foreign Ministers’ meeting with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu hosted by Mr. Rubio in Atlanta.

The Quad Ministers earlier met in Delhi in May this year but could not schedule a summit of the leaders in India, whose turn it has been to host the summit since 2024. Instead, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, U.S. President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will hold a Quad leaders’ meeting in Manila, on the sidelines of the ASEAN-East Asian Summits, that they are all attending in mid-November. In particular, officials are working on ways to take the three key outcomes of the May Quad Foreign Ministers’ meeting forward, including an Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Initiative, the Quad Critical Minerals Framework and the Quad Initiative on Indo-Pacific Energy Security. The decision to hold the Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines, is a first in a non-Quad country and indicates the difficulties the grouping has had in scheduling the summit in the past few years.

In Atlanta, the controversy over the U.S.’s decision to exclude South Africa from the G20 this year due to bilateral tensions, is also expected to be raised by many of the members. India has thus far not commented on the issue, although others like Russia have criticised the U.S. for the decision, and last week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for the U.S. to revoke its decision.
When asked, an official said that India has “always supported an inclusive G20”.

All eyes will also be on any possible trilateral meeting between Mr. Rubio and his counterparts from Russia Sergey Lavrov and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the G20 Ministers’ meeting. On Monday (October 26), Mr. Trump suggested he was open to holding a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping when he travels to Shenzhen, China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum’s summit between December 18 and 19, after the Manila visit.

Mr. Trump will host the G20 summit from December 14 to 15 at the 800-acre Trump National Doral resort owned by the U.S. President. Mr. Modi will travel to the U.S. as part of a three-stop tour, first to Canada from December 11 to 13, then to the U.S., and after that will fly to Brussels, Belgium to sign the India-EU Free Trade Agreement on December 16.

articles.title: Science is successful only when it benefits society: PM Modi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) said science succeeds only when it travels from the laboratory to the land and improves people’s lives.
Addressing the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC), he said it must not become “merely a forum for discussion” but should deliver measurable outcomes.

Mr. Modi said India’s science and technology story has long been one of catching up with other countries, but in the 21st century the country has emerged as a leader in scientific and technological developments. He said, “The discovery of zero showed that India has a culture of discovery. Chandrayaan’s landing near the lunar south pole, Mangalyaan’s success on the first attempt, and the vaccines developed during the COVID-19 pandemic are examples of this.”
The audience at the conclave comprised three Nobel Laureates, top technocrats of India’s scientific establishment, startup founders and scientists from both India and abroad.
Mr. Modi said a country’s technological capabilities depend on its research. He said efforts are underway to “speed up” the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF).

Referring to research funding, he cited a commitment of ₹1 lakh crore, including ₹12,000 crore for taking research from the laboratory to the market, with private investors partnering equally. He also referred to new commitments of ₹24,000 crore.

The number of patents filed in India had risen from about 50,000 to 1.5 lakh, Mr. Modi said, describing this as evidence of a strengthening culture of innovation rather than merely an increase in number.

On Artificial Intelligence (AI), he posed what he called an “important question” about how to exercise scientific judgement in the age of AI. “Science works by questioning paradigms and looking at problems with fresh eyes,” he said. “AI can perform routine tasks quickly and raise productivity, but should not limit scientists’ thinking or independent thought, and its answers must meet the accuracy standards of scientists.”

Referring to the birth anniversary of nuclear scientist Homi J. Bhabha on October 30, Mr. Modi said a developed India will need large quantities of nuclear energy. He noted that the 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) has reached first criticality, strengthening the country’s long-term energy position.

He also pointed to Indian space start-ups, a rocket made in India that placed a satellite in orbit on its first attempt, and the country’s satellite docking capability. Indian-made AI chips are reaching other countries, an AI model has been built domestically, and work is underway on battery technology based on Indian raw materials, he said. The needs of sectors ranging from nuclear energy to space to AI and semiconductors differ, he said, but India’s emerging technologies are rising together.
Describing India as a young country with vision and imagination, he said it needs a generation capable of leading in technology. He summed up the guiding principle as: “We will do it.”

articles.title: Nobel laureate Richard Roberts says it’s ‘nonsense’ to fear foreign dependence due to genetically modified crop use
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Richard J. Roberts, the 1993 Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine, on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) dismissed as “nonsense” the idea that Indians adopting genetically modified crops would become dependent on foreign companies. The work can be done in, and owned by, Indian laboratories, he said.

Dr. Roberts was delivering a plenary address at the second Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC), where scientists and technologists from across India gather over three days at Bharat Mandapam. ESTIC is a replacement for the Indian Science Congress, which was last held in 2023 after disagreements between the Department of Science and Technology and the Indian Science Congress Association.

In his address, he rejected the term ‘genetically modified’ as “very misleading” and referred to such crops throughout as “biotechnologically modified,” or BM, arguing that “every life form on this planet has been genetically modified by evolution.”

Asked about fears that an American corporation such as Monsanto (whose operations were subsumed into that of agrochemicals giant Bayer) could control the seed supply and erode the country’s independence, Dr. Roberts replied: “I think it’s nonsense. You can do improved agriculture here in the labs in India and own everything here in India. You don’t have to go to America or Europe or anywhere else to make CRISPR-modified plants. Anybody can do it. You go to a lab, learn how to do it — maybe it takes you six to eight weeks — and then you can do it. It’s really very straightforward because we’ve come a long way in knowing how to improve crops. But you can own it here in India. You don’t have to go to America or Europe or anywhere else.”

CRISPR is a gene-editing tool in which a guide RNA steers the Cas9 enzyme to a chosen spot in an organism’s DNA, where it cuts, letting scientists alter or insert genes at that site. The foundational CRISPR-Cas9 patents, however, are embroiled in an intellectual property dispute.

GM food crops have a contested history in India. In 2010, then-Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh imposed an indefinite moratorium on Bt brinjal, a genetically-modified variant of the vegetable. This was after years of debate on its safety, the financial impact on farmers, and the implications of foreign ownership of the genetic modification technology. In July 2024, the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict on GM mustard’s environmental release, but unanimously asked the Centre to frame a national policy on GM crops. Golden Rice, engineered in 1999 by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer to carry a vitamin A precursor in its grain, has also proved divisive.

Indian researchers reported in the peer-reviewed PLOS One journal in 2017 that backcrossing one Golden Rice transgene event into an Indian variety had yielded stunted, low-yielding plants, unfit for cultivation despite their high provitamin A content.

Asked whether Golden Rice could disturb India’s agricultural systems, citing the invasive spread of eucalyptus. Dr. Roberts said “he was not an expert in agriculture,” underlining that “there are people out there who truly are experts, who I guess can probably answer the questions that you have much better than I can.”

India permits Bt cotton for commercial cultivation, but no GM food crop. Although the Department of Biotechnology promotes GM crops, their commercial release needs the Environment Minister’s approval, and the Minister is not bound by the regulator’s recommendation, as the Bt brinjal moratorium showed.

Kavitha Kuruganti, who leads the Coalition for a GM-Free India, has previously argued that the yield claims for GM mustard, which was cleared by a technical body but whose release subsequently stalled, are not supported by the developers’ own data. India needs a biosafety policy rather than a policy on GM crops, she said.

Dr. Roberts framed GM as a question of food and nutritional security. “Food is medicine,” he said, for people who cannot afford supplements or drugs. Crops eaten in developing countries, he argued, never received the breeding investment Western staples did because their farmers could not pay for it. “Golden Rice is not priced above ordinary rice, and several Indian government institutes hold licences for it,” he claimed.
He added that Bt brinjal lifted yields in Bangladesh and that “no problem” had been seen in 35 years of GM food.
