articles.title: Lula’s win gives Brazil an opportunity to cement its climate leadership, but challenges remain
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva winning his fourth term as Brazil’s President has also interrupted a series of right-wing electoral wins in Latin America. That said, Brazil and Mexico are now the sole left-wing governments among the region’s largest economies. And while it would be reductive to believe the left is more welcoming of climate action and the right is more disdainful, Mr. Lula also faces significant challenges in his role on the issue both in Brazil and beyond.

His foremost opportunity will be to have Brazil cement its mantle of leadership. Brazil is somewhat unique: it is Latin America’s largest economy, the world’s fifth-largest by area, host to most of the Amazon and, crucially, has diplomatic relationships with the European Union, the U.S., China, the BRICS countries, and many other developing economies — potentially allowing Mr. Lula to negotiate across the divides that currently frustrate climate agreements. In fact, China has made tariffs on clean energy technologies a priority for the COP31 summit, set to commence in under a fortnight in Türkiye, with Beijing arguing against protectionist trade measures while the EU and the U.S. have raised concerns about dependence on Chinese manufacturers.

On the regional level, Brazil straddles several problems, including deforestation in the Amazon, illegal mining, forest fires, and a degrading river basin, that demand region-wide cooperation, including the representation of Indigenous groups. Mr. Lula revived such cooperation to a commendable degree through the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organisation (ACTO), by hosting the Belém summit in 2023, and by making further commitments at the Bogotá summit in 2025.

However, the optimism Mr. Lula warrants is tempered by the Belém Declaration in 2023 failing to establish a binding collective deadline to end deforestation in the Amazon rainforest and to prohibit the development of new oil projects in the region. Both the dependence of the Amazonian countries on agriculture, petroleum, and mining and the powers and resources available to their regulators are markedly different, and political changes are not conducive to sustaining regional cooperation.

Mr. Lula’s fourth term could thus keep ACTO going, especially on cross-border enforcement and in preserving a forum for governments to negotiate on conflicting political priorities. But given the divergent economic incentives and weak national institutions, lasting change means ACTO also developing common monitoring and financing arrangements.

On a more global level, Brazil has come to play a major role in climate negotiations because of its simultaneous status as a major oil producer and, especially under Lula, a strong advocate of international climate cooperation.

In fact, the day after Mr. Lula’s election win, the Netherlands announced that it intends to contribute up to $500 million over a decade, on certain conditions, to Brazil’s ‘Tropical Forest Forever Facility’ (TFFF). The pledge brings the sum of commitments announced thus far to $7.8 billion, against the target of $10 billion by the end of 2026. Lula’s continuing government will help establish the TFFF in its formative years and steady its hand as a potentially new international financial institution.

In the same spirit, Colombia and the Netherlands convened the first international conference dedicated to transitioning away from fossil fuels in April. Fifty-seven countries, including Brazil, participated to develop proposals for financial cooperation, among other matters, and planned for a second meeting in 2027.

As well, at the COP30 climate talks that Brazil presided over last year, Mr. Lula supported proposals to develop an international roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, drawing support from more than 80 countries, but the summit could not see through due to opposition from Russia and Saudi Arabia, among others. The April conference has thus emerged as a parallel mechanism to effect action.

Yet another avenue in the same vein is the EU-Mercosur relationship. The EU and the South American trade bloc signed their interim trade and partnership agreements in January. The latter’s ratification will be significant because they require governments to comply with the Paris Agreement — and could allow Mr. Lula’s climate diplomacy to work through UN negotiations as well as trade and investment relationships to create longer-lasting economic commitments. On the flip side, it may also create greater incentives to convert forestland for other use, so Lula and his peers will have to institute more effective protections.

All this said, while preserving cooperation is essential to effective climate action, it will amount to little if it does not also cut emissions. In fact, continuity in international climate diplomacy could prevent regression without also yielding the acceleration required to meet climate goals. The UN Environment Programme has already found that even if all countries deliver on their pledges vis-à-vis the Paris Agreement, the world is on course to warming by 2.6°C by the end of the century.

Brazil’s incoming conservative Congress is also likely to constrain the Lula government’s ability to sustain expenditure — even if his term provides continuity through 2030, an important year that numerous climate-related commitments use as a deadline or milestone year. That Mr. Lula’s win is a record also raises the prospect of policy whiplash, especially against programmes that depend on his personal political authority, when his last term ends.

articles.title: India must make its defence chips end-to-end, say scientists
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: India’s increasingly network-centric weapons, from the BrahMos cruise missile to the proposed Sudarshan Chakra air defence shield, will remain vulnerable so long as the semiconductors inside them are imported, senior defence scientists said on Tuesday, calling for chips to be designed, manufactured and packaged end-to-end in the country.

Speaking at the ‘Chips for the Next Battlefield: Semiconductors, AI & the Future of Defense’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, former Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) Director General V.K. Saraswat said warfare had moved from platform-centric fighting to network-centric operations, in which command, control and communications riding on semiconductors decide the outcome.

“What you saw in Operation Sindoor … is that we are today more or less equipped with complete network-centric capability,” Dr. Saraswat said. Sudarshan Chakra, the multi-layer, multi-domain air defence system announced by the Prime Minister, would fuse data from satellite, sea, air and land-based sensors using artificial intelligence-enabled software, he added. “But we have realised that is not enough for future warfare, for long-duration warfare, to take care of saturation attacks.” Drone swarms, he noted, now arrive “in hundreds and thousands”, and directed energy weapons were needed alongside ballistic missile defence.

A. Sivathanu Pillai, founder, CEO and Managing Director of BrahMos Aerospace, said precision was the point at which chips entered the picture. A BrahMos missile given a target’s coordinates changes course within milliseconds to secure a “bullseye hit”, he said. “How has the intelligence come to that? It is a processor and the software. So semiconductors play a very important role there.” He added that the Light Combat Aircraft Mark 2 could, on a single mission, process as much data as the entire MiG-21 fleet processed in 1971, and that even Chandrayaan-3’s landing was achieved with semiconductor systems that “was all imported, you know; that was our problem”.

Most Indian defence systems are based on 28-nanometre chips, Dr. Pillai said, while the world has moved to 3 nanometres. India is compensating for weaker hardware with software — for instance, by collating data from multiple GPS sources because it does not have a military satellite giving it military-specification accuracy, but that approach would not be enough for hypersonic systems, he argued.

“The government has said that 3 nanometre we will achieve sometime around 2030 to 35. That is too late in the present situation,” Dr. Pillai said, warning that controls on materials, devices and chip-making equipment were coming. “If you want to wait for 2030 to 35 to achieve it, you will miss the bus.” The equipment needed to make a foundry, and not just the foundry itself, would also have to be produced in India, he said.

Dr. Saraswat added that advanced nodes of 5, 3 and 2 nanometres would be essential for AI systems, including large language models and AI at the edge, even if 28-nanometre chips, and perhaps 14-nanometre chips, could carry today’s Sudarshan Chakra requirements.

Deleep Nair, Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras, traced how far behind domestic fabrication remains. India received complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology from the Radio Corporation of America before Taiwan did, he said, but the Semiconductor Complex Limited (SCL) in Chandigarh was shut for a long period after a fire in the late 1980s. The leading-edge technology running in India today, at SCL, is 180 nanometres, he said, which is the same that Intel, AMD and IBM had in the mid-1990s. Under the DRDO, the Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre (GAETEC) works on gallium arsenide and gallium nitride, he added.

That dependence carries a security risk, Dr. Saraswat said, recalling how supplies of the 8086/8087 processors used in the first Prithvi missile were curtailed once the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme was announced, and dried up further under the Missile Technology Control Regime. “These devices, if they are compromised while they are being manufactured, then your weapon is compromised,” he said, citing Stuxnet, in which a flaw introduced during fabrication allowed a controller running centrifuges at an Iranian enrichment plant to be remotely overrun. Communication links, foreign cloud infrastructure and foreign GPS-based position, navigation and timing systems posed the same problem, he said: “If the cloud is sitting outside, the entire information going through my network-centric warfare system through the cloud, I am compromised.”

The prescription from the panel was end-to-end domestic capability under the India Semiconductor Mission covering materials, design, manufacturing, equipment and human resources, including compound semiconductors such as gallium nitride and silicon carbide, which sit at the front end of radars and imaging systems. The waiting line for extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment needed for advanced nodes was already four to five years, Dr. Saraswat noted.

Both he and Dr. Pillai called for research and development fabs in the IITs and other universities, on the model of Belgium’s Interuniversity Microelectronics Centre, warning that without them India would again have to import technology for the next generation, such as neuromorphic chips. Dr. Pillai said India already accounted for 20% of the world’s chip design capability. “Why not go in a big way to develop the manpower? Instead of 20%, let us take 50% of the design we should do for the world,” he said, adding that universities should also take up packaging and testing.

Dr. Nair said the Tata fab in Gujarat, being set up with a technology licence from Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, would bring the 40-nanometre node, on which a lot of applications could run, while packaging plants were coming up under the mission.

articles.title: India must build semiconductor capabilities beyond chip design, says DG of Semiconductor Laboratory
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: India needs to strengthen capabilities across the semiconductor value chain, from manufacturing and materials to research and specialised skills, to reduce dependence on foreign technologies and build a resilient domestic ecosystem, Dr. Kamaljeet Singh, Director-General of the Semiconductor Laboratory (SCL), Mohali, said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

Speaking at the inaugural session of the Semiconductor Summit 2026, organised by SRM Institute of Science and Technology in association with The Hindu , he said India had a significant presence in semiconductor design but remained dependent on foreign suppliers for critical inputs, including electronic design automation (EDA) tools.
“But the EDA tools which we are using also come from the U.S. So that is why all dependencies are foreign,” he said.

Mr. Singh said the country needed to overcome several challenges to become a technological power. “Technology is one of the challenges, talent is one of the challenges, resources is one of the challenges, time is the challenge, acceptability is the challenge and capital is the challenge,” he said.

He said India needed to build capabilities not only in chip design and fabrication but also in the supporting supply chain, including manufacturing equipment, raw materials, chemicals, gases and packaging materials. Semiconductor supply chains were concentrated in a small number of countries, making access to these inputs critical, he said.
India’s semiconductor requirements were substantial, and the country needed to manufacture more of the chips it used domestically, Mr. Singh said.

He highlighted the need to connect research with manufacturing, arguing that developing semiconductor technologies required researchers, pilot lines, manufacturing facilities and industry participation.
“You need a lot of researchers to come into place, you need a manufacturing unit, you need a lot of technology to be developed to attain the system design and architecture,” he said.

Mr. Singh said the India Semiconductor Mission had supported the development of domestic capabilities. Under the first phase, ₹76,000 crore had been pumped in, with 12 projects approved, five of which had been operationalised and another expected to become operational, he said.

The second phase of the mission had six pillars, including chip design, manufacturing, materials and machinery, with research and development and skill development added as two further areas of focus, he said.
He stressed that India needed to strengthen specialised engineering and manufacturing capabilities alongside its existing design talent.

Mr. Singh highlighted SCL’s efforts to make semiconductor design education more accessible through open-source tools. The laboratory had integrated its process design kit (PDK) with open-source tools so that students unable to afford commercial EDA software could learn chip design.

articles.title: A final surge: On Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: On the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: Wicked surprise: On the northeast monsoon
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: As India recovers from a monsoon-deficit year , there is both hope and trepidation regarding the prospects for that ‘other monsoon’, or the ‘northeast monsoon’ . While contributing only around a quarter of India’s annual rainfall, it is largely focused on the south-east peninsula regions of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Keralam. The southwest monsoon, influenced by a strengthening El Niño , has already left its desiccating mark. Rainfall from June-September was 759.4 mm against 868.6 mm, a 12.6% deficit, the driest in 11 years. This has impacted kharif sowing and is reflected in food inflation.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said that this year, the northeast monsoon rainfall, spanning October to December, would likely be ‘normal’ , meaning in line with a 50-year average and within a 12% error window. Most parts of the country, it said, are expected to receive below-normal rainfall, except some areas of northwest India and southern parts of peninsular India, where rainfall is likely to be normal to above-normal. The wide error window, however, is far less precise than its forecasts for the southwest monsoon with its margin of 5%, and can sometimes make the northeast monsoon the bearer of nasty surprises. For instance, December 1, 2015, saw the city of Chennai deluged by its heaviest rainfall in 24-hours in over a century ; at least 500 lives were lost and 18 lakh people displaced in the State. That year and the present are linked by a common thread: a powerful El Niño. Associated with the heating up of the Central Pacific, the El Niño is linked to the drying up of the southwest monsoon rains but also yoked — not always — with a vigorous northeast monsoon. Other than in 2015, several El Niño years, such as 1997 and 2009, have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu though El Niño years, such as 2002 and 1982, saw a poor northeast monsoon (and a predictably bad southwest monsoon). While the climate mechanisms linking a vigorous northeast monsoon and El Niño are still to be fully understood, it appears the warming patterns of the El Niño tend to deflect rain-bearing cyclonic circulations in unpredictable ways. Therefore, the Centre and the southern States ought to take enough precautions: from clearing up stormwater drains, fortifying shelters, making provisions for infrastructure damage and tightening weather warning forecasts to prepare for torrents.

articles.title: Old values, new avenues: On India-Poland ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Sixteen years after his visit as Poland’s Prime Minister, Donald Tusk’s travel to Delhi and Bengaluru last week was to signal a renewed desire to work closely with India. Mr. Tusk’s visit, two months ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s trip to Brussels to sign the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement , indicated one part of his agenda. Both sides agreed that it was time to develop trade, currently worth just $6 billion, to double its size by 2030. Mr. Tusk’s last visit to India was in 2017, as President of the European Council for the EU-India summit, and it is fitting that his trip was just as the FTA is finalised and ratified after years of delays. Another area of increased India-Poland collaboration is in technology, AI and defence hardware, critical minerals, renewable and nuclear energy given Poland’s expertise in the last few decades and India’s capacity for scale. As the EU’s sixth largest economy, Poland has officially crossed the $1 trillion GDP (nominal terms) milestone. Its $120-billion-dollar tech economy is also gaining global interest. A large part of Polish machinery and parts is exported to Germany, which in turn has a growing share of Indian imports, and India could consider more trilateral collaborations for manufacturing and mining technology. The two sides agreed to establish a “Defence Industry Dialogue” and explore a dialogue on counter-terrorism cooperation. Finally, the Modi-Tusk talks focused on geopolitics, particularly the ongoing war in Ukraine. The war’s impact, especially on the Global South, has been a concern for India, and the Modi government’s initiative to work on an agreement acceptable to Kyiv and Moscow on grain exports and seafarers’ safety was discussed. The four-pronged plan, announced by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during his September visit to Warsaw, won Mr. Tusk’s support.

At the India-Poland Business Forum in Bengaluru, Mr. Tusk, who was accompanied by a Polish business delegation, said the challenge now was in “translating” the talks and MoUs signed into actual joint ventures between businesses. Apart from the distance and geographies, there is the matter of trust, given India’s defence engagement with Russia and Poland’s defence ties with Pakistan. Poland is credited with training Pakistan’s Air Force in its early years; a mutual defence cooperation agreement was signed in 2018. India has a unique and enduring partnership with Russia, and New Delhi is unlikely to accept Warsaw’s strictures over its military engagement and exercises with Russia that caused a controversy earlier this year during the Polish Foreign Minister’s visit. It is essential for Delhi and Warsaw to complete the confidentiality of classified information that is still being negotiated and draw up the parameters of future cooperation based on realities. Mr. Tusk’s statement that India and Poland today have no “conflicts of interest” is a significant aspiration, for two countries that share old values, and new avenues of partnership.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.
• The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

articles.title: Jain seer gives Karnataka govt. 10-day deadline to meet demands; threatens sallekhana in December if demands remain unmet
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Acharya Gunadharanandi Maharaj of Varur Navagraha Teertha Kshetra has given the State government 10 days to provide written assurances on five demands of the Jain community, including the establishment of a Jain Development Corporation.
He warned that he would intensify an agitation in stages and undertake sallekhana (a Jain religious vow involving voluntary fasting unto death) in December if the demands were not met.

Addressing a press conference in Hubballi on Tuesday, he said the government had failed to take decisive action despite repeated representations over the past three years. He said he could no longer remain a silent spectator to what he described as injustice to the Jain community.

The jain monk said the agitation would begin if the government failed to provide a clear written assurance within 10 days. A march and satyagraha would be organised in November, and he would consider undertaking sallekhana in December if the government continued to remain unresponsive.

The five demands include setting up an independent Jain Development Corporation or board; introducing a special security mechanism for the safe movement of Jain monks and nuns; framing regulations to protect Jain pilgrimage centres, temples and historic religious institutions; providing annual free pilgrimage to Shri Sammed Shikharji for economically weaker Jain devotees; and establishing government rest houses or temporary night shelters along the routes used by monks and nuns.

He urged the government to convene a high-level meeting and constitute a joint committee comprising community representatives and officials from the departments concerned. The government should also provide a written response within 10 days, specifying the status of each demand, the department responsible and a timeline for implementation, he said.

If the government failed to respond positively, the first phase of the agitation would involve foot marches to the residences of MLAs in Jamkhandi, Teradal, Kagwad, Athani, Chikkodi, Nipani, Hukkeri and Belagavi to submit memoranda. This would be followed by a large-scale foot march from Chikkodi to Belagavi and a satyagraha, he said.
The agitation would remain entirely non-violent and would not target any political party, he said, appealing to legislators across party lines to support the community’s demands.

The acharya said the demands concerned the development of the Jain community, the safety of monks and nuns, and the protection of its religious heritage. The government should move beyond assurances and provide a written commitment with a clear implementation schedule, he added.

articles.title: A.P. teachers’ body demands implementation of Old Pension Scheme
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The A.P. United Teachers’ Federation (APUTF) on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) demanded that the Central and State governments protect public education and implement the Old Pension Scheme for government employees.

Speaking at a protest at Dharna Chowk in Vijayawada, as part of a nationwide teachers protest staged under the banner of South Teachers’ Federation of India, the APUTF State president N. Venkateswarlu and general secretary K.S.S. Prasad said that the Central and State governments were systematically undermining public education while favouring private institutions.
They alleged that the government was deliberately weakening the public education system, despite the presence of a large number of students from disadvantaged backgrounds in government schools.

The federation leaders expressed concern over the closure and merger of government schools. Citing a NITI Aayog report, they said approximately 90,000 primary schools had been closed or merged with other schools. They said according to U-DISE Plus reports, 972 primary schools had been unofficially closed over the preceding two years and that government schools accounted for only 42% of students, highlighting the need to strengthen public education.

The federation demanded that 6% of GDP be allocated to education and that 30% of the State budget be earmarked for it. They also called for the provision of adequate staff in government schools, including secondary, upper-primary, and primary school teachers, as well as other essential personnel. They demanded that recruitment of teachers should be completed within six months and that promotions should also be provided.

The federation leaders also demanded timely filling of teacher vacancies in government schools and called for the recruitment of teachers through a Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) and a District Selection Committee (DSC), along with the appointment of special teachers and other necessary staff.

The protest was attended by State leaders and representatives of the federation, including K. Suresh Kumar, A.S. Kanaka Mahalakshmi, Kodikonda Reddy Mohan Rao, B. Lakshma Raju, S.P. Manohar Kumar, N. Satyasri, K.V. Uma Maheswara Rao, B. Subba Reddy, B.V. Ramana, N.S. Koteswara Rao, T.V.V.B. R. R. Chakravarthy, P. Jayakar, Sheikh Jabi, N. Ravi, K. Srinivasa Rao, and representatives from 28 districts, along with other office-bearers and State committee members.

articles.title: On the question of KIIFB’s future
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: In July, Keralam’s newly elected UDF government set up an expert panel to review the functioning of Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB). The panel, headed by a former civil servant, was tasked with recommending measures to restructure KIIFB and strengthen the government’s institutional capabilities, among other things. The committee has recently submitted its report, which has been tabled in the State Assembly.

Apparently critical of KIIFB’s functioning, the committee has recommended winding it up; absorbing its functions and capabilities into the State government, news reports say. The principal reason for the panel’s recommendation is that with the clubbing of KIIFB’s borrowing function with the State budget, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) has lost its primary purpose.

KIIFB, restructured by the LDF government, reportedly boosted the State’s infrastructure investment by raising extra-budgetary resources, including securing soft loans known as “Masala Bonds” from international agencies after the disastrous floods of 2019. However, the SPV’s functioning and financial performance have remained contentious. The comptroller and auditor general’s (CAG) strictures against KIIFB have become a convenient beating stick for the Centre and the Opposition parties in the State. Leftist critics have branded it as the arm of “the Left Managerial State” for promoting controversial projects, bypassing legislative approvals. In the fog of the debate, KIIFB’s original purpose and economic principles underlying it seem to have been lost sight of. We seek to explain them, intending to shed some light on the contentious issue.

Though Keralam has sound traditional transport infrastructure such as road network and rail connectivity, it lags behind in modern facilities, such as high-speed railways or highways, especially when compared to the neighbouring States. Keralam reportedly spends a mere 1.5 per cent of the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) on infrastructure. This was so in spite of Keralam’s own-tax revenue to GSDP ratio being among the highest among major States, as per the RBI data.

KIIFB was set up in 1999 and underwent a major restructuring in 2016; the institution’s record in expanding public goods is apparently well acknowledged. However, its functioning raised many queries. The CAG found that the SPV’s finances flouted its procedural audits, which became a sticking point between the Centre and the State. Moreover, as KIIFB functioned outside the purview of the State budget, without generating financial profits from its lending, its borrowings being serviced out of the State’s revenue became the heart of the contention.

In the good/bad old days of “planning”, State finances broadly followed the “gap-filling” approach; meaning the Centre made up the difference between a State’s projected revenue growth and its “developmental needs” as per the State plans. It was a negotiated process, part financial and part political. Evidence shows that richer and politically influential States got the lion’s share of the divisible pool of the plan resources.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM) 2003 changed that by seemingly imposing a “hard budget constraint”, with the fiscal deficit capped at 3 per cent of GSDP. The RBI now monitors the size of the State debt. The coupon (interest) rate of the State loans depends on the State’s debt sustainability measures. The hard budget constraint has reportedly improved State finances, or at a minimum, made them transparent.

However, most States have devised a variety of means for securing extra-budgetary resources, or off-budget borrowings (OBBs) – as evident from the RBI’s compilation of State finances. The CAG, tracking OBBs, finds that there is a bewildering variety of them. And the actual OBBs are far higher than what it is able to count, as per its own findings. In other words, ensuring fiscal discipline seems like a cat-and-mouse game between the Centre and States. Incidentally, Keralam is not among the worst offenders.

Globally, a variety of financial institutions and fiscal arrangements have existed outside of the budgetary process. Numerous kinds of para-statal organisations are a feature – not a bug – of the fiscal landscape, especially among fast-growing Asian economies. China, for instance, has a bewildering variety of financial arrangements that enable provinces to draw resources from the national development banks to sustain employment at the local level, augment production and exports and ensure political stability. No wonder, China’s public debt to GDP ratio is nearly 300 per cent – though most of it domestic.

Then, realistically, what should be the rules for managing extra-budgetary resources and institutions for Keralam? Simply speaking, if extra-budgetary resources are productively used and they comply with the government expenditure principles, having such off-budget institutions/borrowings may not be undesirable. This follows the Domar rule: so long as the output growth rate exceeds the interest rate on such loans (either at current or at constant prices), they are being used productively. Since such investments have a public good character, individual projects may not be yielding adequate revenue or covering the full costs. However, if in the aggregate they contribute to growth in state output (GSDP) and follow the Domar rule, then such investments are in principle viable.

However, if the State-level SPVs borrow from external sources for social purposes or green financing, which usually have lower interest rates for longer maturities, they need to be assessed differently, as they involve exchange rate risk. Given Keralam’s fragile ecology and need for substantial low-cost resources for protecting it, external borrowing for such purposes by creating SPVs may be desirable, as KIIFB reportedly proved to be after the floods in 2019. The expert committee’s recommendation to dissolve KIIFB is the easier part. In the present political milieu, efforts to boost public investments to catch up with the neighbouring States are a harder job – with the Centre strictly monitoring Keralam. The State will have to devise newer and administratively innovative means to tap OBBs, as most States do. The task is primarily a political one.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh braces for 11th very severe cyclonic storm
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Andhra Pradesh has experienced 61 cyclonic storms since 1970, but only a few have intensified into Very Severe Cyclonic Storms (VSCS). The State is now bracing for one such storm, Arnab, nearly eight years after Titli struck in October 2018.

According to the India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) records of cyclonic storms that affected the Andhra Pradesh coast between 1970 and 2023, the State witnessed 10 Very Severe Cyclonic Storms during the period. Arnab would be the 11th, if it reaches this intensity.

The IMD classifies cyclonic storms based on their maximum sustained wind speeds. A cyclonic storm has wind speeds of 62-88 kmph, a severe cyclonic storm 89-117 kmph, and a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm 118-167 kmph. An Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds of 168-221 kmph, while a Super Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds exceeding 221 kmph.

The 10 previous VSCS events occurred in 1999, 2000, 2011, 2013, 2014 and 2018. The year 2013 alone witnessed three such storms: Phailin in October, Lehar in November and Madi in December. In 2014, Hudhud caused extensive damage in Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Srikakulam and East Godavari districts.

According to a case study by C. Hari Kiran of the Andhra Pradesh State Development Planning Society (APSDPS), Hudhud recorded wind speeds of 181.6 kmph. Phailin was even more intense, with wind speeds of 200-210 kmph. Weather models indicate that Arnab may be less intense, with its maximum wind speed expected to be around 140 kmph.
The last Very Severe Cyclonic Storm to affect the State, according to the IMD records, was Titli, which formed over the Bay of Bengal in October 2018 and made landfall near Palasa.
More recent cyclones, including Montha and Michaung, were classified as Severe Cyclonic Storms.

articles.title: BJP protests Kharge’s remark on PM’s father in Bihar and Jharkhand
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) units in Bihar and Jharkhand on Monday (October 26, 2026) staged protests against Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his controversial remark, “ Modi ka baap bhi jayega ” (Modi’s father will also be defeated), made at a party event in Patna. BJP leaders and workers in both States took out marches and burnt effigies of the Congress leader.

In Patna, hundreds of BJP workers, led by State unit president Sanjay Saraogi, took to the streets and raised slogans against Mr. Kharge. Before burning his effigy, some protesters slapped it to register their protest. They also carried placards and posters bearing slogans against Congress leader Rahul Gandhi.

The protesters gathered near the State BJP office and marched through the Income Tax roundabout to Dak Bungalow Chauraha, where they burnt an effigy of the Congress president. Several senior party leaders and office-bearers, including Cooperative Minister Ram Kripal Yadav and MLA and Chief Whip Sanjeev Chaurasia, participated in the protest.

Slamming the Congress, Mr. Saraogi said, “One may disagree with the Prime Minister’s politics, but the use of derogatory language regarding his late parents is unacceptable under any circumstances. This is not the first time indecent language has been used on the soil of Bihar concerning the Prime Minister’s late mother as well.”

He recalled that derogatory remarks against the Prime Minister’s mother had previously been made in his home district of Darbhanga. Mr. Saraogi said that remarks about a deceased family member violate political decorum, and the people of Bihar would not tolerate such language.

“The frustration felt by the Congress and the ‘ Mahagathbandhan ’ [Grand Alliance] leaders is due to rejection by the public. Instead of addressing issues of public concern from political platforms, Congress leaders are showing their frustration through inappropriate and undignified remarks,” Mr. Saraogi said.
He expressed confidence that the public would respond democratically and that the Congress would have to face the political consequences of the remarks.

Hundreds of BJP workers gathered at the District School premises near Shaheed Chowk before marching towards the Congress office, raising slogans against the party.

“Prime Minister Narendra Modi was elected through the mandate of the people. While opposing his political views and policies is a democratic right, making indecent remarks at a personal or familial level under the guise of opposition is, under no circumstances, acceptable,” Mr. Sahu said.

Mr. Marandi also termed the remarks inappropriate and unfortunate. He demanded that either the Congress or Mr. Kharge apologise to the nation immediately. He said Mr. Modi is not merely a BJP leader but a democratically elected Prime Minister who represents the country’s 1.4 billion citizens.

articles.title: H.K. Patil sees need for setting up irrigation study centre to honour V.V. Deshpande
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: There is a need to set up an irrigation study centre in the name of irrigation expert Vithalrao Vaikunthrao Deshpande either in the Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU), Belagavi, or the Karnatak University, Dharwad, the former Irrigation Minister H.K. Patil said in Dharwad on Sunday.
Mr. Patil called for the establishment of the centre that will take up research and extension activities in North Karnataka.
“It should be named after Deshpande to honour his outstanding contributions to the development of irrigation in the State,” he said.
“A study centre in his name will help preserve his achievements and inspire future generations of engineers,” he said.
He was speaking at the birth centenary celebration of the late V.V. Deshpande, organised in collaboration with various engineers associations at Alur Venkatrao Bhavan there.

Deshpande who belonged to Haliyal in Uttar Kannada had played a significant role in several major irrigation projects, including the Ghataprabha, the Malaprabha, the Bhadra and the Kali. “However, despite his exceptional engineering contributions, we have failed in adequately recognising his services,” he said.
He admitted that even during his tenure as Water Resources Minister, sufficient efforts were not made to honour Deshpande’s legacy.

“I have seen that officials who had worked with him fondly referred to him as Annadata. Beyond his engineering expertise, Deshpande empowered farmers by helping create irrigation infrastructure essential for agricultural prosperity. However, he did not receive the recognition he deserved from the administration and society,” he said.
He thanked the organisers for celebrating Deshpande’s birth centenary.
On behalf of the Deshpande family, the Lifetime Achievement Award was presented to retired engineer M.B. Parappagowda, while Jagadish Nandi received the Award for Excellence in Civil Engineering.
MLA Arvind Bellad, who felicitated the award winners, praised Rajan Deshpande for honouring his father’s legacy through the awards and encouraging professionals in the field of engineering.
Mr. Bellad observed that standards of integrity and excellence in society, administration and politics have declined over the years.

articles.title: MSMEs seek improvement of electricity infrastructure in Coimbatore district
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Tamil Nadu Association of Cottage and Tiny Enterprises, representing micro industries in Coimbatore city, has appealed to the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited to strengthen the electricity infrastructure in Coimbatore district.

Its president J. James said in a press release on Monday that given the high concentration of small-scale industrial units alongside residential areas in the district, additional dedicated 11 kV/22 kV power lines should be connected to all 110 kV substations to prevent power outages during the summer season. The power lines established for this purpose should not exceed a maximum length of five km as currently, some extend up to approximately 12 km.

In Coimbatore city and surrounding town panchayats and panchayats, new, high-capacity, and high-quality transformers should be erected to address voltage fluctuations. All power lines and sub-stations should be inter-connected to allow flexible routing. In the event of a fault, the affected section should be isolated while ensuring an uninterrupted power supply to the remaining areas.

The Ring Main Units (RMUs) and automatic switches installed by the Energy Department in the district require better maintenance. ‘Fault Off-Call’ (FOC) service specifically for addressing night hour power outages should be established in all areas and circles surrounding Coimbatore city.

In Tamil Nadu, there are over one lakh LTCT (Low Tension Current Transformer) electricity connections, supporting more than 10 lakh micro and small-scale entrepreneurs. Since September 2023, the fixed charge (demand charge) has been increased from ₹35 per kilowatt to ₹162 per kilowatt. On July 29, 2026, the Association representatives submitted a memorandum to the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu requesting that the fixed charge be reverted to the previous rate of ₹35 per kilowatt (for a sanctioned load of up to 112 kW). Although the Chief Minister assured us that action would be taken, this has not yet been implemented. In the interest of the welfare of micro and small-scale entrepreneurs, the demand charges should be reduced for the LT CT industries.

The conductors of existing High Tension (HT) power lines must be upgraded to ensure the entire line can withstand maximum current loads. Further, the capacity of existing distribution transformers should be increased to facilitate higher power distribution.

articles.title: Very severe cyclone ‘Arnab’ to make landfall near Yanam-Kakinada; red alert issued for seven districts
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: As the cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’, which formed over the Bay of Bengal on Monday morning, gets closer to the land and is expected to intensify into ‘severe cyclonic storm’ by Monday night, the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Amaravati, has issued red alerts for seven of the 28 districts in Andhra Pradesh for October 27 (Tuesday).

Isolated extremely heavy rainfall, of 200 mm or more, is likely in the districts of Kakinada, East Godavari, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Eluru, West Godavari, Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR), Anakapalli, while heavy to very heavy rainfall, of around 70 mm to 200 mm, is likely in the districts of Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, NTR, Krishna, Guntur, Bapatla, Srikakulam, Parvathipuram Manyam on Tuesday.

According to the updated information from the IMD, the storm is likely to cross the coast as a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’, with wind speed gusting to 140 kmph, close to Yanam or Kakinada in Andhra Pradesh around noon on October 28 (Wednesday).
As part of its preparedness, the State has already deputed seven National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and eight (SDRF) battalions to districts likely to be affected.

By 2.30 p.m. on Monday, the cyclonic storm lay centered over westcentral and adjoining eastcentral Bay of Bengal, which is about 520 km southeast of Gopalpur in Odisha, 540 km east-southeast of Vishakhapatnam, 620 km east-southeast of Kakinada, 720 km east-southeast of Machilipatnam, 790 km east-southeast of Bapatla and 680 km northwest of Sri Vijaya Puram in the Andaman islands.

The IMD said it will move west-northwestwards, intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal by Monday evening, and further strengthen to form ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ by Tuesday. Thereafter, the system, moving northwestwards, will cross the coast close to Yanam as a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ with the maximum sustained wind speed of 115-125 kmph gusting to 140 kmph by Wednesday noon.

On Monday, the State experienced sweltering heat in many parts, with the day’s maximum temperature reaching 38.4 degree Celsius at Deverapalle in Anakapalli district. A few stations in the districts of Kurnool, NTR, Prakasam, and East Godavari recorded more than 37 degree Celsius. Not a single station recorded rainfall of above 2 mm till 5 p.m., according to real-time rainfall information available on the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES).
However, intense spells of rain are expected later in the evening or at night, as the system strengthens further.

The thunderstorm activity in the State is also likely to begin by Monday night. The A.P. State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) has cautioned the public as gale winds, with speed reaching 90-100 kmph, gusting to 110 kmph, are likely over coastal Andhra Pradesh, while strong winds of speed reaching up to 50 kmph are likely over Rayalaseema.
Fishermen have been strongly warned against venturing into the sea, as the condition is going to be very rough along the A.P. coast. By October 27 evening, it may worsen further.
For any assistance, the public can contact 112, 1070, 18004250101.
Meanwhile, Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has ordered heightened preparedness across the State in view of the threat posed by very severe cyclonic storm Arnab.

articles.title: UPI and the cost of policy reversal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The government has just given itself the legal room to tax the very payment habit it spent a decade building. Tucked into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which would allow the government to notify charges on specified electronic payment modes. The number being proposed is a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The official stand is that this threshold would touch only about five per cent of transactions by volume, sparing the milk-and-vegetable payments that make up the bulk of UPI’s use. But it would cover roughly 65% of transaction value, which is precisely why it matters.
This is not a small, technical fix. It runs counter to a decade-long policy commitment and deserves more scrutiny than it has received.

Consider the arc. Demonetisation in November 2016 was justified, among other things, as a push towards a less-cash economy. UPI, launched earlier that year, became the vehicle for that push, and its zero-MDR regime was a deliberate subsidy to get merchants and consumers off cash. It worked spectacularly. UPI now processes more transactions each month than most of the world’s card networks combined. Having successfully weaned the country away from cash and towards electronic payments, the government now wants to undercut the very success it engineered.

There seems to be a continued pattern of privileging one payment mode over others via policy. India has long taxed even credit cards. Credit card interest and fees attract 18% GST, making the use of credit cards unnecessarily costly. Taxing interest on revolving credit is unusual by international standards; most jurisdictions treat consumer credit interest as a private financial cost, not a taxable service. India taxes it as if using a credit card itself is a luxury.

Now UPI, the payment rail the government spent political capital promoting, is in line for similar treatment. The pattern suggests a need for a more coherent payments policy than giving in to the temptation to tax every transaction that can be observed.
There are at least two problems with this specific move beyond the optics.

First, basic economic theory tells us that the person on whom a tax is levied and the person who actually bears its cost are not always the same. Moreover, UPI or any payments interface is a two-sided market, and taxing two-sided markets is genuinely tricky.

The MDR would nominally fall on merchants, as argued by the government, collected via banks and the National Payments Corporation of India’s ecosystem. But whether that cost gets passed through to merchants, on to consumers, or absorbed by banks and payment service providers depends on competitive intensity on each side of the market. Banks and fintechs compete for merchant relationships and cannot easily raise prices without losing volume to a rival offering free UPI acceptance.

The more likely outcome is that intermediaries — the banks and PSPs that built and maintain the plumbing — absorb the cost, which erodes their incentive to invest in reliability, fraud prevention and expansion into underserved segments. A tax that cannot be reliably passed through does not disappear; it most likely shows up later as degraded service or slower innovation. This is completely counterintuitive if government is proposing this tax as necessary to fund the next stage of UPI growth.

Second, UPI has done real work on financial inclusion at the margin. It has pulled informal transactions into a recorded, traceable digital trail — the very outcome that formalisation and tax-compliance advocates have wanted for years. There have also been attempts to provide credit based on the digital trail created by electronic payments. Every rupee that moves through UPI instead of cash is a rupee the financial institutions can eventually see and use to build a spending profile.

Charging the rail directly could undercut the incentive to use it, cutting against long-standing financial inclusion goals. The government does not need to raise revenue from every rupee that moves electronically; it needs those rupees to keep moving electronically, because that is what delivers the inclusion and compliance dividends it has been chasing since 2016.

Ideally, which payment mode to adopt should be an economic decision for participating actors. Factors such as the size of the business, consumer preferences, and relative cost of using alternative payment systems should determine their usage. Deliberate policy intervention and the current government’s war on cash tilted the scales in favour of UPI. Taxing it now — however nominal or small — could change its usage patterns, and policymakers should not be surprised if one outcome is reduced UPI usage.

articles.title: How India’s life insurance sector funds government expenditure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: When the government borrows, the question that follows is rarely asked aloud: who lends? A large part of the answer is the life insurance sector. Every year, millions of households across India pay premiums into life insurance policies. That money is reinvested, for decades, in the very securities that finance government expenditure — roads, railways, water supplies, hospitals, defence. The household protecting itself against the loss of its breadwinner is simultaneously, and unknowingly, lending to the sovereign [the Central government]. Life insurers collectively hold close to a quarter of India’s outstanding central government dated securities, based on RBI and IRDAI data — a share that has remained stable even as the total sovereign debt stock expanded by around 40 per cent in three years. This is not a number that appears in budget speeches or parliamentary debates. It is, however, a number that matters.

The stoic and resilient quality of the sector’s sovereign support is as significant as its scale. Life insurers write policies with tenures of twenty, thirty, sometimes forty years. Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market. Unlike foreign portfolio investors, whose appetite fluctuates with global risk sentiment, insurance companies buy and hold. They do not exit when oil prices rise or when a geopolitical event triggers a reassessment of emerging market exposure. Their participation is counter-cyclical by design — stable precisely when other buyers become unreliable. A steady domestic base of long-horizon holders reduces rollover risk and moderates borrowing costs across the maturity spectrum.
Life insurers buy when others sell, hold when others exit, and reinvest when others pause. That is the structural consequence of writing long-duration promises to millions of policyholders.

The sector’s contribution is not evenly distributed. The Life Insurance Corporation of India carries the dominant share — a consequence of its scale, its predominantly participating product mix, and the duration of its in-force book. Its March 2025 regulatory filing with IRDAI (Form L-26) confirms that sovereign paper accounts for nearly 63 per cent of its non-linked policyholder corpus — well above the regulatory minimum, and a direct expression of what long-duration liabilities demand at scale.

LIC holds approximately 19 per cent of all outstanding central government dated securities — a figure confirmed by the RBI’s Public Debt Management Quarterly Report for FY24, the most recently published data. LIC’s IRDAI regulatory filings for March 2025 give the institutional reality in absolute terms: ₹20.2 lakh crore in central government securities alone, and ₹32.3 lakh crore in total government and government-guaranteed securities across all funds. These are not estimates. They are figures LIC files with its regulator every quarter and that any researcher can access on the IRDAI website. This makes LIC the single largest institutional holder of Indian government’s debt.
Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market.

Private life insurers, with a higher proportion of unit-linked and shorter-tenure products, contribute a smaller fraction today. As they grow and deepen their traditional offerings, their sovereign allocations will follow the same structural logic.

The regulator has already recognised the systemic dimension of this function: IRDAI designates LIC as a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer every year, describing it as an institution whose distress would cause significant dislocation in the financial system. That designation, rightly made on insurance-sector grounds, points toward a wider truth — the dislocation would extend into the sovereign borrowing programme itself.

Insurers in Japan, the United Kingdom, and South Korea are among the largest holders of their respective governments’ long-dated securities, not because regulation mandates it but because their liability profiles demand it. India’s life insurance sector is following the same path.

India’s life insurance penetration stood at 2.7 per cent of GDP in FY25, the third consecutive year of decline from a pandemic-era peak of 3.2 per cent, against a global life average of 3.0 per cent. Three regulatory interventions between 2023 and 2024 — restructured distribution economics, taxation on certain high-value policies, and mandatory product repricing, simultaneously, has compressed new businesses. While each was defensible in isolation, their cumulative effect was adverse. The sector is recovering. But the episode illustrates a risk worth noting: when multiple regulatory actions compress new business at once, the household savings that would otherwise have flowed into the sovereign debt market through insurance, reduce or find shorter-duration homes elsewhere. The sovereign borrowing programme may not notice this in the short term. Over a decade, it would.
Banking commands policy attention in proportion to its systemic importance. Insurance, which quietly holds close to a quarter of outstanding central government dated securities, does not.

The case for deeper insurance penetration is most often made in the language of household financial protection — the uninsured family, the inadequate sum assured, a mis-sold product or an unsettled claim. These are legitimate concerns. But there is a parallel case, made in the language of sovereign fiscal stability, that has not been fully articulated in public policy discourse. If the reliability of India’s domestic sovereign funding base is a macroeconomic priority given the scale of annual borrowing requirements, then the depth and health of the life insurance sector remain directly relevant to that priority.

articles.title: Swiping in dark: The hidden cost of plastic money
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: A smartwatch bought on impulse, a costly phone ordered just for the thrill of owning it, a festive sale too tempting to resist. In isolation, each swipe may seem harmless, yet the danger lies in accumulation. Money spent in moments of desire can quietly turn into a burden that outlasts the fleeting gratification. Small indulgences, if they add up to a sizeable bill, can take a toll on the monthly budget and derail carefully planned financial goals.
The litmus test comes knocking much later, after the swipes have ended: a shocking bill. Now, to overcome the shock, cardholders often look for a shortcut: paying just the minimum due.

The minimum-due loop is one of the most deceptive traps of a credit card. Paying only this negligible fraction may help avert immediate late-payment penalties and default notices. However, it allows the bulk of your debt to linger and compound.

Crucially, carrying a due attracts interest and simultaneously revokes the interest-free grace period for subsequent purchases. Any new spend begins accruing interest charges immediately at typical annual rates of 36% to 42%, compounded monthly, until the entire bill is cleared in full. If the minimum-due route is a slow leak, ignoring the bill payment entirely is an outright rupture. Failing to pay the minimum due carries far more severe consequences.

The bank would immediately flag the account as overdue, levying hefty late-payment penalties on top of the standard charges. If the default crosses a stipulated time, the bank reports the delinquency to CIBIL and other credit bureaus, leaving a long-lasting scar on your score.

When the bill is bulky, cardholders often lean towards another tempting escape hatch: easy EMIs. Converting a purchase into equated monthly instalments does not erase the cost; rather, it locks you into a high-margin contract.
You forfeit the upfront discounts that are often bundled with full payment, while a relentless 18% GST is slapped onto the interest portion of every single EMI.
By splitting past impulse purchases across future months, you silently mortgage your upcoming cash flows. The bitter truth: the thrill of owning fades fast, but the bill of burden goes on and on.

Paying your bill on time is only half the battle. Even if you are punctual in clearing the bills, it’s not a total financial hygiene. When the usage on your card is close to its ceiling, you trigger an alarm button inside credit bureaus. Lenders gauge your financial stability through credit utilisation, and crossing the 30% threshold paints a picture of being cash hungry. Even if you do not default payment, a high usage of credit erodes your CIBIL score rating, transforming routine swipes into a hidden roadblock when you eventually apply for a home or vehicle loan.
Gliding your credit card smoothly into an ATM for quick cash would force you to endure a rough patch with huge money leaks.

On most credit cards, cash withdrawals carry zero grace period, meaning standard interest rates of 36 to 42% begin compounding moments after the currency is dispensed. Even on select promotional cards that tout an interest-free window, the fixed fees bite hard.

For instance, banks usually cap single ATM withdrawals at ₹10,000 while levying a flat processing fee of around ₹199 plus GST on every single attempt. Therefore, a requirement of ₹50,000 forces you to glide into the vending tunnel five times, instantly draining roughly over ₹1,000 in raw processing charges alone.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.
